hints: Focus on what it means when a halogen molecule forms a new product, it has oxidised the other halide ion by taking its electrons.
Notice that $Y_2$ displaces both $X^-$ and $Z^-$, while $X_2$ displaces nothing, so $Y_2$ is the strongest oxidiser and $X_2$ is the weakest.
Remember the strongest oxidising halogen has the weakest reducing halide ion, so flip the $Y_2 > Z_2 > X_2$ order to rank the ions as reducing agents.
walkthrough:
**Understand what displacement tells us**

A reaction like $X_2$ formed means the added halogen has oxidised the halide ion. The stronger oxidising agent (halogen molecule) wins and forces the other out.

General rule:
$$Halogen_2 + 2Halide^- \rightarrow displaced\ Halogen_2 + 2new\ Halide^-$$

**Rank the halogens as oxidising agents**

Look down each row. $Y_2(aq)$ causes two reactions, forming $X_2$ and $Z_2$. $Z_2(aq)$ causes one reaction, forming $X_2$. $X_2(aq)$ causes zero reactions.

So oxidising strength is:
$$Y_2 > Z_2 > X_2$$

**Flip the order for reducing agents**

A good oxidiser is easily reduced, so its own ion is reluctant to give up electrons. That means oxidising strength and reducing strength are opposite.

So the ions in order of decreasing reducing strength (strongest giver of electrons first) is:
$$X^- > Z^- > Y^-$$

options.A: Incorrect. This puts $Y^-$ in the middle, but $Y_2$ displaces both other ions so $Y_2$ is the strongest oxidiser. That makes $Y^-$ the weakest reducer, not the middle one.
options.B: Correct. $Y_2$ displaces $X^-$ and $Z^-$, and $Z_2$ displaces $X^-$ only, so oxidising power is $Y_2 > Z_2 > X_2$. Reversing this gives reducing power $X^- > Z^- > Y^-$.
options.C: Incorrect. This is the exact reverse of the truth. It treats $Y^-$ as the strongest reducer, but since $Y_2$ is the strongest oxidiser, $Y^-$ must be the weakest reducer.
options.D: Incorrect. This correctly puts $Y^-$ weakest, but swaps $X^-$ and $Z^-$. Since $Z_2$ oxidises $X^-$ to $X_2$, $X^-$ gives up electrons more easily, so $X^-$ is a stronger reducer than $Z^-$.
